newsitem.title: USA: More rain poses new threat to flooded Kentucky.
newsitem.headline: More rain poses new threat to flooded Kentucky.

text.p: More rain fell in the flood-stricken Ohio River Valley on Sunday, posing the threat of flash flooding and slowing the monumental clean-up effort from the worst deluge in more than three decades.
Amid light rainfall, the Ohio River's highest crest since 1964 slowly edged westward along the Kentucky-Indiana border, inundating more communities as it spilled out of its banks.
"There is rain that stretches over the areas that don't need it," forecaster Scott Yuknis of Weather Services Corp. said.

The National Weather Service issued flash flood warnings for southern Indiana as a line of thunderstorms bore down on the region, although forecasters said the worst-hit areas may be spared the worst of it.
Yuknis said the storm system was weakening and gathering speed as it moved over the area. "The heaviest rain should stay north of the Ohio River Valley and it should move through quickly," he said.

Forecasts called for the rest of the week to remain dry, as the wet weather pattern that pulled moisture up from the Gulf of Mexico into the nation's midsection may be shifting. Dense storms last weekend dumped up to a foot (30 cm) of rain on Louisville, triggering flash floods and sending rivers and streams cascading into the countryside.

In addition, the crest of the Ohio River was driving through a hillier landscape where most homes were on hillsides and should escape the floodwaters, said Alden Taylor of Indiana's Emergency Management Agency.
"The topography changes. There are steeper hills overlooking the river," he noted.
"A lot of homes are still wet and there there are still homes (in eastern Indiana) with water in them," Taylor said of the gradually receding floodwaters.

Schools in parts of southern Indiana that have been closed since the flooding began were preparing to open again by Tuesday once road inspections proved it would be safe for school buses, Taylor said.

Sunday's rainstorms broke a three-day dry spell that allowed tens of thousands of residents back into their ruined homes and begin the rebuilding process -- with many residents expected to move to higher ground.

"Somebody can tell me I can rebuild, but I will not do it," Cora Ferguson of hard-hit Falmouth, Kentucky, said. "I will not come back to Falmouth. It's stupid to rebuild and then the spring rains come and it happens all over again."
Ferguson and her husband own a dozen flood-damaged rental properties in Falmouth, a town of 2,300 ravaged by the Licking River about 40 miles (65 km) southeast of Cincinnati.
Overall damage estimates along the Ohio River and its tributaries ranged upward of $500 million in Kentucky, Ohio, West Virginia and Indiana. The death toll from the floods stood at 31.
Officials estimated that in Kentucky, at least 75,000 homes and businesses were damaged or destroyed. In Ohio, 5,600 homes and businesses sustained heavy damage.

Even with the possibility of more than an inch (2.5 cm) of rain late on Sunday, meteorologists stuck with their prediction that the Ohio River at Cincinnati would fall below flood stage of 52 feet (15.85 metres) Monday as it descended from a crest of 64.7 feet (19.70 metres) earlier this week -- the highest flood level in 33 years.
Overflowing tributaries of the Ohio River, which generated the worst flooding conditions, already have returned to their banks.

Some flood victims managed to joke amid their tears. Richard Craig, a resident of the tiny riverside community of California, Ohio, on the eastern edge of Cincinnati, said while surveying the muddy mess in his home, "I want you to know -- my wife's a better housekeeper than this."
